Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 3, 2023, thunderstorms brought torrential rain, with totals ranging from 2 to 4 inches, to the central and southern South Plains of Texas. [25] This downpour resulted in widespread street flooding in Lubbock, prompting the closure of Southbound US 87 at FM 41 in Lubbock County. [25] The significant runoff also caused the gauge on the North Fork Double Mountain Fork of the Brazos River, located four miles east-southeast of Lubbock, to rise into a minor flood stage. [25] <2> A rapid attribution study by the European group ClimaMeter concluded that the storm system causing major flooding in New York City on September 29, 2023, was 10-20% wetter due to the influence of climate change. The analysis, published in early October 2023, highlighted that a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, leading to more intense rainfall. <3> In a forecast published on October 2, 2023, NOAA predicted a likelihood of high-tide flooding for the entire month of October 2023 in several Virginia locations due to extreme tides. Specifically, Lewisetta was expected to experience potential flooding for the entire month. Windmill Point was also predicted to have flooding for all of October, with the exception of October 7-9. <4> On September 29, 2023, a low-pressure system that absorbed the remnants of Tropical Storm Ophelia caused one of New York City's wettest days in decades, leading to significant flash flooding across the metropolitan area. The torrential rainfall prompted New York Governor Kathy Hochul to declare a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island, and the Hudson Valley. The deluge inundated streets and major highways, including the FDR Drive and Prospect Expressway, forcing road closures and stranding vehicles. The city's public transit was severely impacted, with major disruptions to the subway system, including full and partial line suspensions, particularly in Brooklyn, and suspensions on all three Metro-North train lines. John F. Kennedy International Airport recorded 8.65 inches of rain, its wettest day on record, surpassing a record set by Hurricane Donna in 1960. Brooklyn was one of the hardest-hit boroughs, with some areas receiving more than seven inches of rain, and one location recording 2.5 inches in a single hour. The flooding also forced the temporary closure of a terminal at LaGuardia Airport. <5> A slow-moving storm system caused significant flash flooding across several states in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic regions of the United States between September 8 and September 13, 2023. [8] The most severe impact was felt in Leominster, Massachusetts, on September 11, where up to 11 inches of rain fell within hours, leading to what the state's governor described as "catastrophic" flooding. [8, 11] This prompted the issuance of a rare flash flood emergency for Leominster and the neighboring city of Fitchburg. [8] The torrential rainfall resulted in widespread damage, including flooded homes and businesses, washed-out roads, and the partial collapse of buildings. [7] A sinkhole notably opened up at a car dealership, swallowing several vehicles. [7, 8] Concerns over the integrity of the Barrett Park Pond Dam, which was already in poor condition, led to the evacuation of residents in low-lying areas. [8, 11] In addition to Massachusetts, significant flooding also impacted other states. In Pennsylvania, heavy rainfall on September 9 led to flash floods in Lackawanna County, requiring the rescue of several motorists. [15] Parts of Connecticut, including West Hartford and Danbury, also experienced substantial flooding on September 13, with submerged vehicles and road closures. [8] A second flash flood emergency was declared for the Baltimore, Maryland, area on September 12. [8] <6> On August 24, 2023, torrential rainfall led to severe flash flooding across the Detroit metropolitan area, with significant impacts in western Wayne and Monroe counties. The flooding prompted widespread road closures, including both directions of I-275 at I-94. Major disruptions occurred at the Detroit Metro Airport (DTW) in Romulus, where flooding blocked traffic and cut off access to the McNamara Terminal for several hours. <7> A glacial lake outburst flood from Suicide Basin, a side basin of the Mendenhall Glacier, caused record-breaking flooding along the Mendenhall River in Juneau, Alaska, between August 4 and August 6, 2023. The basin's release of water into Mendenhall Lake began on the evening of August 3rd, with the lake starting to rise by early August 4th. The floodwaters peaked on Saturday, August 5, 2023, with the Mendenhall Lake gauge cresting at 14.97 feet around 11:15 p.m. AKDT. This shattered the previous record of 11.99 feet from July 2016 by nearly three feet. The event caused significant erosion, with one climate specialist noting that "decades worth of erosion happened in one weekend." The powerful flood destroyed homes and other structures, sweeping them into the river and prompting a local emergency declaration. <8> Severe thunderstorms on Saturday, August 5, 2023, brought heavy rain and flash flooding to northwest Iowa. [5, 6] Sioux County was particularly hard-hit, with the city of Sioux Center receiving over seven inches of rain, which caused extensive street flooding and forced road closures. [5] The Sioux County Sheriff also reported street flooding in the communities of Orange City, Hull, Boyden, Rock Valley, and Maurice. [5] In addition to the flooding, a tornado was confirmed by spotters southwest of Sioux Center, though no major damage from it was reported. [5] <9> On the night of August 4, 2023, the city of Kirksville in northern Missouri experienced a significant flash flood after receiving over six inches of rain. The widespread flooding caused major damage to numerous homes and businesses. The Kirksville Fire Department conducted approximately 10 water rescues as the storm system moved through the area. The National Weather Service had reported widespread flash flooding in Kirksville late that evening.

[5, 17] In response, the Arizona National Guard was activated, launching a large-scale rescue operation. This severe weather prompted Texas Governor Greg Abbott to issue a disaster declaration on April 30, 2024, for numerous counties, certifying that the event began on April 26 and was causing widespread property damage. The storms were characterized by significant rainfall, leading to flash flooding concerns, alongside the threat of large hail and damaging winds. <10> A severe weather outbreak on April 10, 2024, struck the Gulf Coast and lower Mississippi Valley, causing a deadly Flash Flood Emergency in New Orleans and surrounding Louisiana parishes. Widespread rainfall totals of 2 to 5 inches were reported, with expected rainfall rates between 0.25 and 1 inch per hour. The NWS warned that flash flooding was already occurring in these areas on Saturday morning. For some parts of Illinois and Missouri, the situation escalated to a Flash Flood Emergency. The severe weather was part of a larger system that prompted flood threats for a wide area stretching from Iowa to Georgia. <2> A major federal disaster declaration was approved for Ohio and Marion counties in West Virginia following severe flash flooding on June 14-15, 2025. The news of the declaration was first reported on July 22, 2025, and was formally declared by the President on July 23. The flooding in Ohio County resulted in nine deaths and destroyed dozens of homes, while Marion County experienced significant property damage. The declaration made Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) assistance available to residents and businesses, including programs for temporary housing and home repairs. The President granted the state $11.7 million in federal disaster aid. <3> The National Weather Service in St. Louis issued a Flash Flood Emergency for central Fayette County, Illinois, on the night of July 20, 2025, lasting into the early hours of July 21. [5] Intense thunderstorms produced significant rainfall, with reports ranging from 5-6 inches to over 7 inches. [5, 7] This led to a "particularly dangerous situation" with severe and life-threatening flash flooding. [5] The affected communities included Vandalia, St. Elmo, Brownstown, and Ramsey, where widespread roadway flooding was confirmed, rendering parts of Interstate 70 impassable. [6, 5] The Weather Prediction Center had placed the region under an Enhanced Risk for excessive rainfall prior to the event. [5] <4> By mid-July 2025, the United States had set a new record for the highest mid-year total of flash flood warnings, with multiple sources reporting totals exceeding 3,000. Environment+Energy Leader reported a specific figure of over 3,160 warnings issued between January and mid-July 2025. This unprecedented number of alerts is attributed to the increasing intensity and frequency of extreme weather events. Experts identify key contributors as a warmer atmosphere, which can hold more moisture, and stalled storm systems. These factors lead to more intense rainfall rates and consequently, faster and more destructive flash flooding. The record-setting pace of warnings reflects broader climate trends, with severe storms and extreme rainfall expected to become more common as global temperatures rise. <5> A tropical disturbance, identified as Invest 93L, brought a surge of tropical moisture and heavy rainfall to the northern Gulf Coast during the week of July 7, 2025. The system, which did not develop into a named tropical storm, moved inland on Thursday, July 10. The most significant impacts were heavy rain and flooding along the Interstate 10 corridor, affecting communities in Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana through at least Saturday, July 12. Flood Watches were issued for parishes along the Gulf Coast in response to the threat. [7, 11] The extreme rainfall led to numerous high-water rescues and significant damage to homes and businesses. [10, 11] Other hard-hit areas included Silver Spring, Maryland, and Great Falls, Virginia. [17] The event was part of a broader period of unsettled weather, with some areas near Petersburg experiencing significant flash flooding on July 13 as well. The event caused significant disruption, closing hundreds of roads and causing power outages. There are conflicting reports on the number of fatalities. However, subsequent reports indicated the death toll had risen to at least six across several counties, including Alamance, Orange, and Chatham. <10> An article published on June 19, 2025, detailed the challenges Flathead County, Montana, is facing in its efforts to plan for future major flood events. This unprecedented number of alerts is attributed to the increasing intensity and frequency of extreme weather events. Experts identify key contributors as a warmer atmosphere, which can hold more moisture, and stalled storm systems.
